name: Convergent Evolution
one_line: Unrelated living things that face the same problem each grow a similar answer.
story: Joseph Anning digs an ichthyosaur skull out of the cliffs at Lyme Regis, and his sister Mary then finds the skeleton; the ichthyosaur's body converged on the dolphin's shape

shallow.scene: In 1811, in Lyme Regis, a small town on the English coast, Joseph Anning dug a long-snouted skull out from under the cliffs. His sister Mary later dug the rest of the skeleton out of the same spot. The animal had a streamlined body and paddle-like limbs, and it was later named the ichthyosaur. Put a drawing of what it looked like next to a dolphin, and the outlines almost line up. But the ichthyosaur was a reptile that swam all over the oceans in the age of the dinosaurs. The dolphin is a mammal, and its ancestors went back from land into the sea tens of millions of years after the ichthyosaurs died out.
shallow.plain: Three boatbuilders who have never met, one on a river bend, one by a lake and one in a sea harbor, all need to build fast boats. None of them has seen the others' plans, yet all three boats come out pointed at both ends and fat in the middle, because a blunt-nosed boat can't be rowed fast. When living things with different ancestors each grow a similar solution, that is called convergent evolution. The ichthyosaur was a reptile and the dolphin is a mammal. Neither copied the other, yet both grew the same body, pointed at both ends and fat in the middle, which suits fast swimming equally well.

deep.mechanism:
### The faster you swim, the less choice of outline you have

The drag of water goes up with the square of speed: double the speed and the drag is about four times as much. Animals that swim slowly feel little drag. A jellyfish drifting and eating plankton, or a manatee slowly chewing seagrass, can survive with a round body or a flat one. Tuna, sharks and dolphins chase schools of fish and feel a lot of drag; a body a little too blunt can't catch up and is weeded out. The more speed is demanded, the fewer shapes can survive, so animals from different origins are squeezed into the same narrow range.

### A likeness counts as convergence only if each grew it separately

The front-limb bones of the ichthyosaur and the dolphin were both inherited from earlier four-legged animals; that part comes from a common ancestor. The paddle-like outline of the flipper, though, the ichthyosaur and the dolphin each grew separately, and that is the convergence. To judge whether a likeness is convergence, fix on one specific feature and ask: did each grow it on its own, or did it come down from an ancestor? On the same flipper, the bones are inherited and the outline grew separately.

### Different starting points give solutions that are only similar

The cactuses of the Americas and some African euphorbias have both grown thick fleshy stems, few leaves and many spines: the thick stem stores water and the spines keep animals from eating it. A cactus's spines grow from a special structure called an areole, and euphorbias don't have one. Each uses parts that came from its own ancestors, so they look alike on the outside but the details don't match.
deep.origin: Convergent evolution comes out of comparative anatomy, and no one person is credited with proposing it. In 1843 Richard Owen told apart homology and analogy: the first is "likeness handed down from an ancestor," the second is "likeness each grew on its own." Later, with the phylogenetic tree, which is a family tree of living things, researchers could check on the tree whether a feature appeared separately on different branches.
deep.limits: Convergence is easiest to see where the demand for speed is high and there are few ways out, such as fast swimming in water or flying in the air. When the demand eases, each grows its own way: jellyfish and manatees, which are in no hurry, share no common outline. And however high the demand, it only narrows the shapes; it doesn't pick one for the animal. To fly, birds have their wings, bats have theirs, and insects have wings of their own.

uses.text: Racing cyclists' helmets in every country taper into a teardrop shape: once the speed goes up, the air allows only a few shapes.
When two teams that don't know each other use the same clumsy method, go and find the wall they both ran into. Where that wall is matters more to note down than the method itself.
When you want to copy what works somewhere else, first write down the hard constraint it depends on, then see whether you have an equally hard one where you are.

examples.title: Cutting messages into small pieces
examples.text: In the early 1960s, Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation in the US was working out how a communications network could still deliver messages after an attack had cut some of its lines. A few years later, Donald Davies at Britain's National Physical Laboratory was thinking about something else: how to let many people share one expensive computer line. At first neither knew about the other, and both cut messages into small pieces that each took their own route and were put back together at the end. Davies named these small pieces "packets."

examples.title: Warehouses moved next to the airport
examples.text: Two wholesalers who don't know each other, one selling fresh flowers and one selling live fish, both moved their warehouses next to the airport cargo area, and both switched to loading at night and delivering before dawn. Flowers and fish both suffer if they spend a night on the road.

examples.title: Stack stone high and you get a pyramid
examples.text: The ancient Egyptians and the Maya of Central America were separated by the Atlantic, and archaeologists have found no accepted evidence of contact between them. Yet on both sides the biggest stone buildings are pyramids, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, stepping in layer by layer. When you stack stone blocks high, a side that is too steep collapses, and this kind of shape is the only one that stands. Around 2600 BC, the Bent Pyramid of the pharaoh Sneferu was laid at about 54 degrees for its lower half, then switched to about 43 degrees halfway up. The usual explanation is that the original slope was too steep to hold. The Red Pyramid, built after it, used 43 degrees from the base up.

ask: Did each of them work out these similar methods on their own, or did someone lead and the others learn from them?
What is the wall they all ran into: time, cost, or physical conditions?
Is that wall just as high where I am?

with.sees: Five bubble-tea shops on one street have all cut their menus to eight drinks. Social proof would say they are copying one another, and following them is just more copying. Convergent evolution would say that if every shop's customers all arrive in the half hour after school lets out, the same problem has pushed them to the same place, and following them makes sense. First ask the owners why they cut the menu. If the answer is "everyone next door did," it's copying; if it's "we can't get through the line in half an hour," each ran into the same wall.

Picture two cities that are both choked by morning rush-hour traffic. One had tram tracks from the early days and expanded them into a subway; the other had none, so it could only paint in bus lanes. Convergent evolution asks what problem the two cities share; path dependence asks what each already had to work with. When the results come out the same, "faster commutes," look at the shared constraint; when the results split apart, look at where each started.

questions.stem: Birds and bats both have wings, and the bones in their front limbs are laid out in a similar way. A classmate says their wings evolved separately and were not handed down from a common ancestor.
questions.question: What justifies saying this?
questions.explain: The question is about one specific feature, the wing surface. The common ancestor of the two was a four-legged animal that couldn't fly, and the wing surface used for flight appeared separately in the two lines; that is what makes it grown separately. The layout of the front-limb bones is a different feature.

options.text: The front-limb bones are laid out similarly, which shows the wings were handed down from an ancestor.
options.feedback: A similar bone layout shows that the front limb as a structure came from a common ancestor. The wing surface is a different feature, and the two can't be lumped together.

options.text: Their common ancestor couldn't fly, and the wing surface appeared separately in each line.
options.feedback: The common ancestor had no wing surface, and one appeared in each line at different times. That is what shows it grew separately.

options.text: Both can fly and the wings do the same job, so they must have grown separately.
options.feedback: Doing the same job isn't enough, because a feature left by a common ancestor can do the same job too. What you need to check is whether the common ancestor had this feature.

options.text: Both live in the sky, and sharing the same surroundings is enough to prove they grew the wings separately.
options.feedback: Sharing the same surroundings is only a clue. You still have to check whether the common ancestor had this feature.

questions.stem: Two convenience-store chains that have nothing to do with each other have both moved their oden counter, the warm pots of simmering snacks, next to the checkout. Someone says that since the two thought it through separately and landed in the same place, this layout must be a good idea. You want to find out first whether each really worked it out on its own.
questions.question: What should you check first?
questions.explain: If the two chains' likeness comes from the same source, you can't say each thought it through separately. Only by tracking down the source can you judge whether it grew independently.

options.text: How many stores each chain has.
options.feedback: How many stores they have has nothing to do with where the two layouts came from.

options.text: Where oden ranks in sales at each chain.
options.feedback: Sales can show whether the layout is worth it, but not whether each chain came up with it separately.

options.text: Whether the two head offices are far apart.
options.feedback: Head offices far apart could still use the same design firm; this clue can't tell you whether each thought it through separately.

options.text: Whether both counter layouts came from the same design firm or the same industry handbook.
options.feedback: If they come from the same source, the two chains are using the same answer, not each running into the same problem.

questions.stem: In a small county town with fierce sunshine, you see that three households who don't know each other have all built houses with thick walls and small windows. You are about to build a house on a damp, rainy coast and want to copy this style directly.
questions.question: What should you ask before you start?
questions.explain: The three households each chose thick walls and small windows, which shows the style deals with a problem they share: keeping out heat. Your problem is damp, so the two sets of walls aren't necessarily dealing with the same thing.

options.text: What the thick walls and small windows keep out, and whether I need to keep out the same thing.
options.feedback: The three households' thick walls and small windows were forced on them by the fierce sun. On the coast the problem is damp, so first see whether what these walls do fits your problem.

options.text: All three built this way, which shows the style works anywhere.
options.feedback: The three ended up in the same place only because they had the same problem. Move somewhere else and the problem changes, so the conclusion can't be carried over directly.

options.text: The coast has sun too, so it's the same problem as the small town.
options.feedback: Having sun doesn't make the problem the same. The hardest thing on the coast is damp, and thick walls and small windows may not help with that.

options.text: Small windows let in little air, but a few fans will fix that, and there's nothing else to check.
options.feedback: Fans only patch one gap. The question is whether this style is aimed at your problem, and that hasn't been checked.

figure.title: 3 fast swimmers, 3 origins, 1 shape; slow ones vary
figure.caption: Manatee and dolphin are both mammals yet look nothing alike; dolphin, tuna and ichthyosaur differ in origin yet share one shape. Speed sets it, not ancestry.
